messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sang is a 35-year-old South Eastern Asian male who works as a UX Designer. Married and deeply thoughtful, Sang’s life was upended when he faced a life-threatening illness that nearly took his life two years ago. The experience has left him with an acute sense of vulnerability and maladaptive coping mechanisms that have significantly impacted his daily functioning. From the outset, Sang had come to believe there was something wrong with him as a person—a deep-seated belief that he was defective and weak. This emotional numbness often made him feel dead inside, leading him to avoid situations where he might confront these feelings head-on. He would avoid hospitals, ambulances, and any physical examinations because of the overwhelming fear they triggered in him. Sang’s negative self-appraisals had led him to isolate himself from such reminders, which only intensified his anxiety. When something took longer than expected—such as a delayed appointment or a routine check-up—he assumed that something bad was happening. This pervasive sense of threat made it impossible for him to trust the assurances of others about his safety. His body felt constantly tense and ready to react to danger, amplifying his fear. The more Sang avoided medical cues and stressful situations, the more convinced he became that they posed an imminent threat to his well-being. The cycle tightened as Sang’s negative appraisals fueled his maladaptive strategies. Every time he encountered a trigger—a siren in the distance, a news report about illness—he would retreat further into avoidance behaviors. His constant state of alertness made it difficult for him to relax or engage fully with life. The more he avoided these situations, the stronger his belief became that there was something fundamentally wrong with him. This pattern of behavior had consequences both professionally and personally. As a UX Designer, Sang’s work often required him to collaborate closely with others and attend meetings where health topics sometimes came up. These interactions were now fraught with anxiety, leading him to avoid participating fully or even missing some critical sessions. At home, his wife noticed that he was becoming increasingly distant and withdrawn, which caused tension in their relationship. Sang’s experience of the traumatic event left a profound mark on his psyche. The memory of being critically ill and nearly dying made hospitals and medical settings particularly potent triggers. He had come to believe that any delay or uncertainty signaled impending doom, reinforcing his sense of weakness and emotional numbness. This belief further fueled his avoidance behaviors, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of fear and isolation. Finally, the cumulative strain became too much for Sang to bear alone. The realization that he was no longer able to function at work without being overwhelmed by anxiety led him to seek help. He was most afraid of being trapped in this state indefinitely, unable to reconnect with his loved ones or enjoy life. What he hoped for was a way to break free from the cycle and reclaim some sense of normalcy. Sang’s current state is marked by an acute awareness that something must change. While he acknowledges the need for help, he remains deeply afraid of confronting the fears that have become so ingrained in his daily existence. The path forward is daunting, but Sang has taken the first step towards healing and reclaiming a life beyond fear.
